source_text:
Κατὰ μὲν οὖν τὸν λόγον τῆς δημιουργίας διωρίσμεθα ἀπὸ
πάντων τῶν ζώων· ἐὰν δὲ ᾖς ἁμαρτωλὸς, πόρ νος, κατωφερὴς, οὐ διωρίσθης ἀπὸ
τετραπόδων γῆς, ἀλλὰ παρασυνεβλήθης τοῖς κτήνεσι, καὶ ἐγένου ὡς 12.1045 ἵππος
καὶ ἡμίονος, οἷς οὐκ ἔστι σύνεσις, καὶ ἵππος θηλυμανής. ΚΕΦ. Μʹ. Μὴ, ἀλλὰ ζῶσαι
ὥσπερ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀσφύν σου. Τὰ μὲν τέλεια τῶν ἀγωνισμάτων τοῖς καλῶς ἀθλή σασι
μετὰ τὸν βίον ἀπόκειται τοῦτον· οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον καὶ ἤδη ἡ χάρις τοῦ Θεοῦ
ἀῤῥαβωνίζεται τοὺς ἀθλη τάς. ∆ιὰ τοῦτο, ὅτε ἠγωνίσατο τὰ μέγιστα ὁ Ἰώβ· ὅτε,
ἀποβαλὼν τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, ἐδόξασε τὸν δεδωκότα· ὅτε, ἀποθέμενος τὰ τέκνα,
εὐχαρίστησε τῷ παρειλη φότι· ὅτε, νοσήσας ὡς σκώληκας ἀνομβρεῖν ἀπὸ τοῦ
σώματος, οὐ νενίκηται ἀπὸ τῶν πόνων· προοίμια καὶ ἀῤῥαβῶνα τῶν ἄθλων δίδωσιν
αὐτῷ ὁ Θεὸς, χρη ματίσας αὐτῷ διὰ νέφους καὶ λαίλαπος. Ἀκούσας οὖν τῶν
προτέρων λόγων, δέον ἀποκρίνασθαι πρὸς Θεὸν, σιωπᾷ, ὡς οὐκ ἔχων παῤῥησίαν·
οὔπω γὰρ ᾔδει τὸ, «Μωσῆς ἐλάλει, ὁ δὲ Θεὸς ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτῷ φωνῇ.» Ὁ μέντοι
Θεὸς δίδωσιν αὐτῷ παῤῥησίαν τοῦ λέγειν· καὶ τοσαύτη ἐστὶν αὐτοῦ ἡ χρηστότης,
ὥστε ἀναλα βεῖν αὐτὸν πρόσωπον οὐ κρίνοντος, ἀλλὰ κρινομένου μετὰ τοῦ
ἀνθρώπου. Καὶ ἄλλαι τοῦτο ἐδίδαξαν Γρα φαί· ὡς τὸ, «∆εῦτε, καὶ διαλεχθῶμεν·» καὶ,
«Λαός μου, τί ἐποίησά σοι;» Ἤδη ἆθλον δίδωσιν αὐτῷ ὁ Θεὸς, ὅτι ἄνθρωπον ἐρωτᾷ,
ὅτι πυνθάνεται αὐτοῦ, ὅτι δίδωσιν ἐξουσίαν τῆς ἀποκρίσεως. Εἰ μὴ ἦν νενι κηκὼς,
οὐκ ἐλάμβανεν· εἰ μὴ ἦν ὑπομείνας, οὐκ ἂν ἤκουσε· «Ζῶσαι ὥσπερ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀσφύν
σου,» καὶ μὴ σιώπα· ἀλλ' ἀνδρίζου πρὸς τὰς ἐρωτήσεις· ὅσῳ γὰρ ὀσφύς τινος οὐκ
ἔζωσται, οὐδὲ συνέσφιγκται, ἀλ λὰ λέλυται, οὐ δύναται εὐλόγως ἀποκρίνασθαι τῷ
Θεῷ. Μὴ πρότερον οὖν ἀποκρινάσθω τις τῷ Θεῷ, ἐὰν μὴ ἀνὴρ γένηται τέλειος τὴν
πνευματικὴν ἡλικίαν καὶ τὴν ὀσφὺν ζώσηται. Μὴ ἀποποιοῦ μου τὸ κρῖμα. Μὴ οἵου
ἀλόγως κεκρίσθαι μοι ταῦτα ἅπερ ὑπέμεινας, μηδὲ ἀποποιοῦ μου τὸ κρῖμα.
thought_title: God gives Job boldness as a prize
orientation: Origen is expounding God's address to Job in Job 40, explaining that God's command to gird the loins is a gift of boldness given to Job as a proven victor.
pass_a_gloss: According to the principle of creation, then, we have been separated from all the animals; but if you are a sinner, a fornicator, downward-bent, you have not been separated from the four-footed creatures of the earth, but you have been compared to the beasts, and you have become like a horse and a mule, in which there is no understanding, and a mare-mad horse. Chapter 40. No, but gird your loins like a man. The perfect [prizes] of the contests are laid up for those who have contended well after this life; but no less even now the grace of God gives an earnest to the athletes. For this reason, when Job contended the greatest things; when, having cast away his possessions, he glorified the one who had given [them]; when, having laid aside his children, he gave thanks to the one who had taken [them]; when, having fallen ill so as to rain worms from his body, he was not conquered by the pains; God gives him preludes and an earnest of the prizes, having addressed him through a cloud and a whirlwind. Having heard, then, the earlier words, though it was necessary to answer God, he is silent, as not having boldness; for he did not yet know the [saying], 'Moses was speaking, and God answered him with a voice.' God, however, gives him boldness to speak; and so great is his kindness that he takes up a person not of a judge, but of one being judged with the human being. And other Scriptures taught this; as the [saying], 'Come, and let us reason together;' and, 'My people, what have I done to you?' Already God gives him a prize, because he questions a human being, because he inquires of him, because he gives authority of the answer. If he had not conquered, he would not have received [it]; if he had not endured, he would not have heard: 'Gird your loins like a man,' and do not be silent; but act like a man toward the questions; for insofar as someone's loins are not girded, nor bound tight, but are loosened, he cannot reasonably answer God. Let no one, then, answer God before he becomes a man perfect in spiritual age and girds his loins. Do not reject my judgment. Do not suppose that these things which you endured have been judged by me without reason, and do not reject my judgment.

choices.why: Keeps the spatial metaphor of being dragged down by sin, which Origen contrasts with the upward dignity of reason.
Preserves the compound's literal force (mad after mares) and its vivid animal imagery.
Keeps the commercial metaphor of a down payment or pledge, which Origen uses for the grace given to athletes before the full prize.
Preserves the musical or rhetorical sense of preliminary movements that anticipate the full contest prizes.
Renders the imperative's call to manly courage, matching the glossary's 'courage' for ἀνδρεία.
Captures the sense of pushing away or disowning God's judgment, which Origen glosses as denying what God has decided.

bible_refs.note: ζῶσαι ὥσπερ ἀνὴρ τὴν ὀσφύν σου
Μωσῆς ἐλάλει, ὁ δὲ Θεὸς ἀπεκρίνατο αὐτῷ φωνῇ

pass_b_english: By the principle of creation, then, we have been separated from all the animals. But if you are a sinner, a fornicator, bent toward earth, you have not been separated from the four-footed creatures of the earth. You have been compared to the beasts, and you have become like a horse and a mule, which have no understanding, and like a horse in heat.

Chapter 40. “No, but gird up your loins like a man” (Job 40:7). The full prizes of the contests are stored up for those who have fought well after this life, but even now the grace of God gives an earnest to the athletes. So when Job fought his greatest contests—when he lost his possessions and glorified the One who gave them; when he laid aside his children and gave thanks to the One who took them; when he fell ill so that worms rained from his body and was not conquered by his pains—God gave him preludes and an earnest of the prizes by addressing him through cloud and whirlwind.

After hearing the earlier words, then, when he ought to answer God, he is silent, as though he did not have boldness. For he did not yet know the saying, “Moses spoke, and God answered him with a voice” (Exodus 19:19). But God gives him boldness to speak, and so great is His kindness that He takes on the role not of a judge but of one being judged alongside the human being. Other Scriptures taught this too, such as, “Come, and let us reason together” (Isaiah 1:18), and, “My people, what have I done to you?” (Micah 6:3).

God is already giving him a prize, because He questions a human being, because He inquires of him, because He gives him authority to answer. If he had not conquered, he would not have received it. If he had not endured, he would not have heard, “Gird up your loins like a man” (Job 40:7), and do not be silent, but act like a man in the face of the questions. For as long as someone's loins are not girded and bound tight but are slack, he cannot answer God with good reason.

Let no one, then, answer God before he has become a man perfect in spiritual stature and has girded his loins. “Do not reject my judgment” (Job 40:8). Do not suppose that what you endured has been judged by me without reason, and do not reject my judgment.

problems.why: Singular and plural forms; reader may not connect 'athletes' to Job.
'Boldness' (parrhesia) is key term; 'uncondemned conscience' describes its basis but may confuse.
Four different terms for same figure; reader may not identify them.
problems.fix: Add note identifying dragon/Satan/devil/tempter as same being.

problems.why: Archaic or obscure term for depraved/sunk in sin; modern reader puzzled.
'Judgment' shifts between meaning a legal verdict, a divine decision, and an acquittal; reader may lose the thread.
problems.fix: Distinguish 'verdict' (athletic/legal) from 'judgment' (God's decree) where the Greek uses different words.

fixed: Glossary 'the perfect athlete': The English uses 'athletes' (plural) for the general class and 'Job' by name for the individual; no change needed.
Glossary 'boldness': The English uses 'boldness' consistently for parrhesia; no change needed.
Glossary 'the dragon': The English does not use 'the dragon' in this section; no change needed.
Mistranslation 'downward-bent': The Greek κατωφερής means 'bent downward' or 'sunk in sin'; 'downward-bent' is obscure, so changed to 'bent toward earth'.
Glossary 'judgment': The English uses 'judgment' consistently for κρῖμα; no change needed.

problems.why: Bizarre compound; 'mare-mad' is not standard English, seems like calque.
problems.fix: Use 'horse in heat' or 'lustful stallion' depending on Greek sense.

problems.why: 'Mare-mad' is archaic/obscure; context needs 'lust-crazed' or 'in heat.'
problems.fix: Use 'like a maddened stallion' or 'like a horse in heat.'

edits.new: and like a horse in heat.

fixed: The Greek ἵππος θηλυμανής means a horse mad after mares, i.e., a lustful stallion or horse in heat. 'Mare-mad' is obscure and not standard English, so I replaced it with 'a horse in heat,' which is clear and natural.

last_rejected.quote: You have been compared to the beasts, and you have become like a horse and a mule
last_rejected.source_quote: παρασυνεβλήθης τοῖς κτήνεσι, καὶ ἐγένου ὡς ἵππος καὶ ἡμίονος
last_rejected.why: Greek says you were led astray by the beasts; English changes agency to a mere comparison.
last_rejected.fix: You have been led astray by the beasts, and you have become like a horse and a mule
last_rejected.ruling: παρασυνεβλήθης is from παρασυμβάλλω, 'be classed/likened with'; 'compared to' fits the horse/mule context, not 'led astray' (παρασύρω).

last_rejected.quote: If he had not conquered, he would not have received it.
last_rejected.source_quote: Εἰ μὴ ἦν νενι κηκὼς, οὐκ ἐλάμβανεν
last_rejected.why: Greek expresses 'if he had not endured', not 'conquered'; the meaning of endurance is altered.
last_rejected.fix: If he had not endured, he would not have received it.
last_rejected.ruling: νενικηκὼς is perfect of νικάω 'conquer'; ὑπομείνας 'endured' is the next clause, rendered separately and correctly.

last_rejected.quote: The full prizes of the contests are stored up for those who have fought well after this life
last_rejected.source_quote: Τὰ μὲν τέλεια τῶν ἀγωνισμάτων τοῖς καλῶς ἀθλήσασι μετὰ τὸν βίον ἀπόκειται τοῦτον
last_rejected.why: “After this life” modifies when the prizes are stored up, not when the athletes fought.
last_rejected.fix: The full prizes of the contests are stored up after this life for those who have fought well.
last_rejected.ruling: The English word order is slightly ambiguous, but "μετὰ τὸν βίον τοῦτον" goes with ἀπόκειται. The next clause, "οὐδὲν δὲ ἧττον καὶ ἤδη" ("even now"), makes the sense clear. This is a stylistic fix.
